description: A study of why nations cooperate and of the major global and regional organisations such as the UN, Commonwealth, NAM, AU, EAC and SADC, including Tanzania's role in them.

mcq.questionText: In which year was the United Nations Organisation formally established?
mcq.explanation: The United Nations was founded in 1945, after the end of the Second World War, to maintain international peace and security.

mcq.questionText: Which UN organ has the main responsibility for maintaining international peace and security?
mcq.explanation: The Security Council is the UN organ charged with maintaining international peace and security, including authorising peacekeeping and sanctions.

mcq.questionText: How many permanent members does the UN Security Council have?
mcq.explanation: The Security Council has five permanent members (USA, UK, France, Russia and China) who hold the power of veto, plus ten non-permanent members.

mcq.questionText: Which UN agency is mainly concerned with the health and welfare of children?
mcq.explanation: UNICEF (United Nations Children's Fund) focuses on the welfare, health, education and protection of children worldwide.

mcq.questionText: The principal judicial organ of the United Nations is the:
mcq.explanation: The International Court of Justice (ICJ), based in The Hague, is the main judicial organ of the UN and settles legal disputes between states.

mcq.questionText: The Organisation of African Unity (OAU) was formed in:
mcq.explanation: The OAU was founded in 1963 in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, to promote African unity and support liberation from colonial rule.

mcq.questionText: The African Union (AU) replaced the OAU in which year?
mcq.explanation: The African Union was officially launched in 2002 in Durban, South Africa, replacing the OAU which had existed since 1963.

mcq.questionText: The first East African Community was established in 1967 by Kenya, Uganda and:
mcq.explanation: The original EAC of 1967 was formed by the three states of Kenya, Uganda and Tanzania.

mcq.questionText: In which year did the original East African Community collapse?
mcq.explanation: The first EAC broke up in 1977 due to political differences, mistrust and unequal sharing of benefits among the member states.

mcq.questionText: The East African Community was revived in:
mcq.explanation: The EAC was re-established in 2000 when the Treaty for its re-establishment came into force, reviving cooperation among Kenya, Uganda and Tanzania.

mcq.questionText: Which organisation is largely made up of Britain and its former colonies?
mcq.explanation: The Commonwealth is a voluntary association mainly of the United Kingdom and its former colonies that cooperate in trade, sports, education and democracy.

mcq.questionText: The Non-Aligned Movement (NAM) was formed during the Cold War mainly to:

options.text: Support the Western bloc against the East
Avoid joining either the Western or Eastern power blocs
Form a military alliance with the Soviet Union

mcq.explanation: NAM was created so that newly independent states could remain neutral and not align with either the capitalist West or the communist East during the Cold War.

mcq.questionText: Which UN agency works to improve food production and fight hunger?
mcq.explanation: The Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO) deals with agriculture, food security and the reduction of hunger and poverty.

mcq.questionText: The Southern African Development Community (SADC) is best described as a:

options.text: Regional economic cooperation organisation in Southern Africa

mcq.explanation: SADC is a regional organisation that promotes economic development, trade and political cooperation among countries in Southern Africa.

mcq.questionText: Which of the following is a major weakness of the United Nations?

options.text: It has too many member states
The veto power of the permanent Security Council members can block decisions
It refuses to allow African members

mcq.explanation: A key weakness of the UN is that any of the five permanent members can use the veto to block action, often paralysing the Security Council.

fib.questionText: The United Nations Organisation was established in the year _____.
fib.explanation: The UN was founded in 1945 after the Second World War to maintain international peace and security.

fib.questionText: The headquarters of the United Nations is located in _____ City, USA.
fib.explanation: The UN headquarters is in New York City, in the United States of America.

fib.questionText: The UN organ in which all member states are represented and each has one vote is the _____.
fib.explanation: In the General Assembly every member state is represented and has an equal single vote.

fib.questionText: The UN agency responsible for international public health is the _____.
fib.explanation: The World Health Organisation (WHO) coordinates global efforts to control disease and improve health.

fib.questionText: The Organisation of African Unity was formed in the year _____.
fib.explanation: The OAU was founded in 1963 in Addis Ababa to promote unity and the liberation of Africa.

fib.questionText: The African Union was officially launched in the year _____, replacing the OAU.
fib.explanation: The AU was launched in 2002 in Durban, South Africa, transforming the former OAU.

fib.questionText: The original East African Community collapsed in the year _____.
fib.explanation: The first EAC fell apart in 1977 because of political differences and unequal benefits among members.

fib.questionText: The East African Community was revived in the year _____.
fib.explanation: The EAC was re-established when its new treaty came into force in 2000.

fib.questionText: The UN agency that promotes education, science and culture is _____.
fib.explanation: UNESCO (United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organisation) promotes cooperation in education, science and culture.

fib.questionText: An association mainly of Britain and its former colonies is known as the _____.
fib.explanation: The Commonwealth is a voluntary association of the United Kingdom and most of its former colonies.

tf.questionText: The United Nations was formed in 1945 to maintain international peace and security.
tf.explanation: The UN was indeed established in 1945, with the maintenance of peace and security as its main aim.

tf.questionText: The Security Council has fifteen permanent members each with the power of veto.
tf.explanation: The Security Council has fifteen members in total, but only five permanent members hold the veto power.

tf.questionText: The African Union was formed in 2002 out of the former Organisation of African Unity.
tf.explanation: The AU replaced the OAU in 2002, building on the OAU founded in 1963.

tf.questionText: Tanzania, Kenya and Uganda were the founding members of the original East African Community of 1967.
tf.explanation: The 1967 EAC was founded by Tanzania, Kenya and Uganda before its collapse in 1977.

tf.questionText: The Non-Aligned Movement was created to join newly independent states firmly to the Western bloc.
tf.explanation: NAM was formed so that members would NOT align with either the Western or Eastern blocs during the Cold War.

tf.questionText: UNICEF is the UN agency that deals mainly with the welfare of children.
tf.explanation: UNICEF focuses on the health, education and protection of children worldwide.

tf.questionText: The International Court of Justice is the principal judicial organ of the United Nations.
tf.explanation: The ICJ, based in The Hague, settles legal disputes between states as the UN's main judicial body.

tf.questionText: SADC is a regional organisation that promotes economic cooperation in West Africa.
tf.explanation: SADC promotes economic and political cooperation in Southern Africa, not West Africa.

tf.questionText: The original East African Community collapsed in 1977 partly because of political differences and unequal sharing of benefits.
tf.explanation: Mistrust, ideological differences and unequal benefits among members contributed to the 1977 collapse of the EAC.

tf.questionText: International cooperation has no benefits for developing countries like Tanzania.
tf.explanation: International cooperation brings benefits such as trade, aid, technology transfer, peace and shared development to countries like Tanzania.

summary.questionText: State the meaning of international cooperation.
summary.correctAnswer: International cooperation is the process by which different countries work together for common goals such as peace, security, trade and development.
summary.explanation: It involves states joining efforts and resources to solve shared problems and advance mutual interests.

summary.questionText: Name the five main organs of the United Nations.
summary.correctAnswer: The General Assembly, the Security Council, the Secretariat, the International Court of Justice and the Economic and Social Council (ECOSOC).
summary.explanation: These are the principal organs of the UN, each with a distinct role in its work.

summary.questionText: Give two main aims of the United Nations.
summary.correctAnswer: To maintain international peace and security, and to promote cooperation in solving economic, social and humanitarian problems.
summary.explanation: The UN also promotes human rights and friendly relations among nations.

summary.questionText: Mention four specialised agencies of the United Nations.
summary.explanation: These agencies handle children's welfare, health, education and food/agriculture respectively.

summary.questionText: State two weaknesses of the United Nations.
summary.correctAnswer: The veto power of the five permanent members can block important decisions, and the UN often depends on powerful states for funds and military support.
summary.explanation: These weaknesses limit the UN's ability to act independently and quickly in crises.

summary.questionText: State two aims of the African Union.
summary.correctAnswer: To promote unity and solidarity among African states, and to accelerate the political and economic integration and development of the continent.
summary.explanation: The AU also works to defend the sovereignty and peace of member states.

summary.questionText: Give two reasons for the collapse of the original East African Community in 1977.
summary.correctAnswer: Political and ideological differences among the member states, and the unequal sharing of benefits from the Community.
summary.explanation: Mistrust between leaders and lack of a strong dispute-settling mechanism also contributed.

summary.questionText: State two benefits of regional integration to member countries.
summary.correctAnswer: It widens the market for goods and increases trade, and it promotes peace, security and joint development among members.
summary.explanation: Regional integration also encourages free movement of people, labour and capital.

summary.questionText: State two challenges facing regional integration in Africa.
summary.correctAnswer: Differences in levels of economic development among members, and the fear of losing national sovereignty or revenue.
summary.explanation: Poor infrastructure, political instability and overlapping memberships also hinder integration.

summary.questionText: Explain Tanzania's role in international cooperation.
summary.correctAnswer: Tanzania has been a founding and active member of organisations such as the OAU/AU, EAC, SADC, the Commonwealth, NAM and the UN, and supported African liberation movements and regional peace.
summary.explanation: Tanzania hosted liberation fighters and promoted unity, making it a strong supporter of cooperation in Africa and beyond.

hoq.questionText: Why might a small developing country like Tanzania consider the veto power in the UN Security Council a weakness of the United Nations?

options.text: Because the veto allows any of the five permanent members to block decisions, so the interests of powerful states can override those of weaker nations
Because the veto gives every member state equal authority in the Assembly
Because the veto increases the number of African permanent members
Because the veto removes the need for a Security Council altogether

hoq.explanation: The veto concentrates power in the five permanent members, meaning that decisions can be blocked by a single great power regardless of the majority, which disadvantages smaller and weaker states.

hoq.questionText: Comparing the collapse of the 1967 EAC with its 2000 revival, which lesson best explains why the revived Community tried to build stronger institutions and treaties?

options.text: Because larger markets always collapse without colonial support
Because the first EAC failed partly from weak structures, mistrust and unequal benefits, so firmer rules were needed to sustain cooperation
Because the revival aimed to exclude Tanzania from membership
Because regional cooperation was banned by the United Nations after 1977

hoq.explanation: The 1977 collapse was caused largely by weak institutions, political mistrust and unequal sharing of benefits, so the revived 2000 EAC emphasised stronger treaties and organs to make integration more durable.

hoq.questionText: Why is the transformation of the OAU (1963) into the AU (2002) seen as a shift towards deeper African integration rather than just a change of name?

options.text: Because the AU abandoned all the goals of the OAU
Because the AU returned Africa to colonial administration
Because the AU added stronger organs and a focus on economic integration, peace-keeping and development beyond the OAU's main task of decolonisation
Because the AU reduced the number of African member states

hoq.explanation: The OAU's chief mission had been ending colonialism; with that largely achieved, the AU broadened the agenda to economic integration, conflict resolution, good governance and development, supported by new organs, marking a deeper form of unity.
